title: Contract infrastructure: AI challenges siloed CLM systems
desc: Contrasts platform replacement, integration and incumbent adaptation without resolving which model best serves broad in-house work.

kps.k: The central dispute concerns who will supply contract infrastructure, not whether businesses still need it.
kps.d: Critics argue that AI exposes longstanding weaknesses in contract lifecycle management (CLM) and could displace incumbent products. Nick Fleisher distinguishes those products from CLM’s enduring purpose; Cecilia Ziniti predicts some companies will use AI directly on document stores while acknowledging CLM’s value for signatures, approvals and reminders. SpotDraft’s Shashank Bijapur takes a stronger continuity position: existing CLM capabilities will underpin conversational contracting. These are competing forecasts about product architecture and vendor survival, not evidence that contract management itself is disappearing.

qs.q: SPEAKER_2 (00:22:53) I don't think the core concepts of what CLM is and what it set out to do are dead.
qs.a: E36 - Too Much FOMO: Why I'm Back on the Legal AI Startup Investor Train with Sandstone CEO Nick Fleisher · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

qs.q: And I do think there will be a generation of companies, excuse me, there will be a generation of companies that skips CLM and goes straight to AI pointed at a doc store.
qs.a: E35 - Are Legal AI Assistants Moving In-House? GC AI Founder Cecilia Ziniti · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

kps.k: The critique targets input-heavy, siloed systems that fit neither business users nor the breadth of in-house work.
kps.d: Jarryd Strydom describes CLMs functioning largely as repositories while email retains working context, limiting legal teams’ strategic insight. Fleisher and Ziniti argue that contract-centric software neglects other legal work and the channels business colleagues already use. An implementation practitioner in “Is AI for Contract Review Exciting?” offers a structural explanation: each team needs flexibility that conflicts with scalable software. Fleisher’s account of a costly, poorly used deployment illustrates the complaint, but neither it nor Strydom’s experience establishes an industry adoption rate.

qs.q: It's the issue that the legal team has tooling that's actually very much siloed from the rest of the business.
qs.a: E43 - AI and the Future of In-House Legal, Sandstone Co-Founder Jarryd Strydom · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

qs.q: What lawyers do in companies goes way beyond contracts, and we just talked about this.
qs.a: E36 - Too Much FOMO: Why I'm Back on the Legal AI Startup Investor Train with Sandstone CEO Nick Fleisher · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

kps.k: AI vendors propose integration, replacement and broader legal-department platforms as distinct routes forward.
kps.d: Sandstone says it analyses data from existing CLMs, allowing customers to preserve investments, although Fleisher reports some full migrations. GC AI reports demand for CLM integration and a customer using AI extraction during migration. Ivo claims repository intelligence attracts customers that already have sophisticated CLMs. Separately, participants predict contract-review tools will expand into CLM functions, while the Wordsmith interview frames purpose-built in-house platforms as a different category altogether. These accounts support coexistence as well as substitution; they do not establish comparative product superiority.

qs.q: We're going to make great use of that data and the way it's structured, and we'll pull it into our system so that we can do the AI analyses and all of the interesting work on top of it.
qs.a: E36 - Too Much FOMO: Why I'm Back on the Legal AI Startup Investor Train with Sandstone CEO Nick Fleisher · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

qs.q: And it's a product that's getting enormous adoption across companies who have pretty robust and sophisticated CLM systems in place already.
qs.a: E39 - AI vs Legacy SaaS in Legal: Min-Kyu Jung, CEO Ivo · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

kps.k: Incumbent adaptation divides advocates of fundamental rebuilding from advocates of embedding AI where it adds value.
kps.d: Min-Kyu Jung argues that existing architecture and recurring revenue create an innovator’s dilemma, but leaves open a CLM comeback after ground-up redesign. Other speakers warn that adding chat or summaries preserves restrictive workflows, extending that criticism to legal-research incumbents. Ironclad’s Jason Boehmig instead describes product-by-product integration guided by user value. The Screens.AI–Agiloft transaction supplies a firsthand example of acquisition as an adaptation route, although the participant attributes its feasibility partly to Agiloft’s capital position. The material does not demonstrate that either rebuilding or incremental integration consistently wins.

qs.q: And I think the leaders there need to have the courage to kind of rip out what they're doing at the moment already and kind of rethink from the ground up, what does a best in class product look like that solves all of these problems if now that we have AI.
qs.a: E39 - AI vs Legacy SaaS in Legal: Min-Kyu Jung, CEO Ivo · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

qs.q: You know, look, I helped Screens.AI sell to Agiloft earlier this year on this premise.
qs.a: E27 - Zach and Richard's Legal AI Adventure: Big Deals and AI Revolution · Market & press · 2025

kps.k: Reported benefits and failures illustrate competing propositions, but do not resolve the performance debate.
kps.d: Ziniti recounts AI extracting migration data that a CLM provider reportedly could not supply or would charge $60,000 to provide. Jung claims analysis across millions of agreements without metadata tagging. Against sweeping accounts of CLM failure, an Ironclad speaker claims contracting runs 80% faster and describes AI suggesting edits for attorney review. None of these excerpts supplies independent comparative testing or measurement methods. Fleisher’s one-hour estimate concerns field mapping, not complete deployment; Bijapur’s separate 80% figure describes a prospective contract-creation workflow, not achieved performance.

qs.q: And their CLM provider said, okay, no, we can't do it or we're in charge of 60 grand professional services to do it.
qs.a: E35 - Are Legal AI Assistants Moving In-House? GC AI Founder Cecilia Ziniti · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

qs.q: We can extract intelligence at scale across millions of agreements.
qs.a: E39 - AI vs Legacy SaaS in Legal: Min-Kyu Jung, CEO Ivo · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

kps.k: AI can weaken CLM purchasing without replacing its functions, while weak investment signals do not prove disappearing demand.
kps.d: Jung identifies competition for legal operations budgets and limited tool-assessment and onboarding capacity. Speakers also report buyers reconsidering purchases and cite funding declines, acquisition down rounds and share-price reactions as warning signs. The contract-review discussion challenges category definitions and offers reputation or enthusiasm for AI as alternative explanations. Eli Amsellem uses the 2020–2022 CLM valuation boom to caution that practical utility does not guarantee attractive legal-AI exit economics. Repeated host criticism and market anecdotes are not independent confirmation of inevitable obsolescence; disclosed CLM holdings and a Sandstone investment also provide relevant context.

qs.q: And even if CLMs are not a direct competitor to a lot of the legal AI tools, they are competing often for the same dollars in the budget, often competing for just the capacity a team has to evaluate a lot of different solutions and on-board different solutions at the same time.
qs.a: E39 - AI vs Legacy SaaS in Legal: Min-Kyu Jung, CEO Ivo · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

qs.q: And maybe the fact that there isn't much investment in CLM is because of the bad rep that it may have built up over the years or because it's much sexier to go with a slinky AI tool right now, fine.
qs.a: Is AI for Contract Review Exciting? · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

kps.k: The practical recommendations favour interoperability, priorities-led purchasing and reconsideration of implementation assumptions.
kps.d: Fleisher proposes reaching business users in existing communication tools; Ziniti similarly prioritises interoperability. “From Legacy Machine Learning to Generative AI” recommends organising a toolkit around business priorities, fragmented records and cross-functional ownership, while questioning long commitments during rapid change. The E37 speaker argues that AI adoption increasingly means directing willing users toward organisational rather than personal tools, not simply persuading reluctant employees to use software. That is a qualitative thesis, not measured behaviour. Together, these recommendations shift attention from category labels and broad rollouts toward workflow fit, implementation burden and usable value.

qs.q: And so basically, like, we need to play nice with all of them.
qs.a: E35 - Are Legal AI Assistants Moving In-House? GC AI Founder Cecilia Ziniti · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

qs.q: And it's a toolkit, you know, it's like, what are your priorities?
qs.a: From Legacy Machine Learning to Generative AI · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

kps.k: The wider argument asks providers to earn continued use through changing customer value, rather than assume incumbency protects them.
kps.d: Fleisher describes switching costs as protection for CLM incumbents. E42 proposes a different basis for durable adoption: communities and collaboration that make products more valuable as usage grows, citing Harvey and Legora’s shared law-firm–client spaces without measuring network effects or retention. The Axiom interview extends adaptation pressure beyond software vendors to ALSPs delivering legal work. Catherine Kemnitz rejects reliance on unchanged services and continued client loyalty; the host locates the pressure in rising expectations rather than inevitable job automation. Neither discussion establishes quantified displacement.

qs.q: So I think the first thing I'll say is companies have spent millions of dollars and many years implementing CLM, and so the biggest moat that the CLMs have is that they're incredibly hard to set up, and they're incredibly hard to rip out.
qs.a: E36 - Too Much FOMO: Why I'm Back on the Legal AI Startup Investor Train with Sandstone CEO Nick Fleisher · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

qs.q: I think that the collaborative elements that they've introduced recently, with shared spaces, that is now allowing for the law firms to essentially offer certain usability to them for their corporate legal customers.
qs.a: E42 - Is Legal AI in Trouble or Just Getting Started? Cosmonauts Founder, Timo Karakashev · Market & press · 2026

vlens.an: This source accepts the proposition that AI exposes weaknesses in incumbent CLM products and leaves unresolved whether they can be successfully rebuilt as AI-first systems. It materially extends the cluster’s argument from contract-software architecture to the provider side: ALSPs and other talent-based professional-services businesses must also reconsider what they deliver and how they deliver it as client standards change. The reasoning is not that automation will necessarily eliminate legal-service jobs, but that unchanged services may cease to meet customer expectations. There is material variation within the interview: the host advances the CLM critique and generalises the risk to ALSPs, while Catherine Kemnitz focuses on Axiom’s management response, endorsing active adaptation while describing opportunities and risks rather than a specific redesign or measured disruption. This single curated source therefore supports a concrete extension of the proposition, but does not establish how widespread that view is among AI-native providers or ALSPs.

qs.q: I certainly could imagine that the CLM is disruptible because I think it had problems even before AI came along.
qs.a: E30 - Is AI Disrupting ALSPs? Axiom CSO Catherine Kemnitz · AI-native providers · 2025

qs.q: I think if we did nothing, if we watched this and thought, no, we're good enough, we can, you know, our clients will sort of keep liking what we do and keep growing the company or whatever, we wouldn't be doing our jobs.
qs.a: E30 - Is AI Disrupting ALSPs? Axiom CSO Catherine Kemnitz · AI-native providers · 2025

vlens.an: This law-firm-voice source accepts the synthesis’s central criticism that AI can expose the limitations of siloed, legacy legal software and materially extends it beyond CLM to incumbent legal-research products. Its main reason is architectural and behavioural: inserting AI into an established product may provide short-term utility, but the surrounding interface and inherited workflows can constrain what the AI enables. The source also argues that incumbents missed opportunities to develop stronger products despite their content advantages. There is some internal qualification: it acknowledges that retrofitting AI can work for a period, while its stronger suggestion that standalone AI may be more valuable remains tentative and is not supported by comparative testing. Thus, it develops the proposition through a cross-category analogy rather than resolving the synthesis’s wider dispute over replacement, integration or incumbent adaptation.

qs.q: So legacy software is like, AI is a square peg in the round hole that is legacy enterprise software.
qs.a: ChatGPT vs. Legal Tech: Who Will Win? · Law firms · 2025

qs.q: But then very quickly, like the AI itself separates and you're sort of stuck in old user behavior.
qs.a: ChatGPT vs. Legal Tech: Who Will Win? · Law firms · 2025

vlens.an: This curated set of market-analyst, consultancy and press voices accepts the synthesis’s core proposition that AI is challenging siloed, burdensome CLM products without eliminating the need for contract infrastructure. It materially develops that proposition by identifying additional mechanisms through which competition may unfold: incumbents may acquire AI-first capabilities; vendors may seek stickiness through user communities and shared law-firm–client workspaces; investors may distinguish practical utility from sustainable application-layer economics; and implementation may shift from persuading reluctant users to steering existing AI demand toward organisation-approved tools. The common reasoning is that incumbency alone will not preserve vendor position: products must create usable value, fit existing workflows and adapt to AI’s different adoption dynamics. There is material internal variation. E27 anticipates AI-first entrants outcompeting some incumbents and possible M&A, but offers this mainly as a forecast, with the Screens.AI–Agiloft transaction as a firsthand yet capital-dependent example. E23 is less architecturally prescriptive and stresses that strong usage appeal does not resolve investment or exit risk. E42 advances a qualitative network-effects thesis rather than measured evidence of retention. E37 focuses on implementation burden and change management, asserting—without quantified adoption data—that AI creates user pull unlike earlier enterprise software. Together these sources extend rather than settle the synthesis’s replacement-versus-integration dispute, and they should not be treated as representative of all analysts, consultancies or press.

qs.q: You know, look, I helped Screens.AI sell to Agiloft earlier this year on this premise.
qs.a: E27 - Zach and Richard's Legal AI Adventure: Big Deals and AI Revolution · Market & press · 2025

qs.q: I think that the collaborative elements that they've introduced recently, with shared spaces, that is now allowing for the law firms to essentially offer certain usability to them for their corporate legal customers.
qs.a: E42 - Is Legal AI in Trouble or Just Getting Started? Cosmonauts Founder, Timo Karakashev · Market & press · 2026

vlens.an: The curated legal-tech vendor sources support the proposition that AI is challenging siloed, input-heavy CLM products without removing the underlying need for contract infrastructure. Their common reasons are that incumbent systems often require substantial user input, preserve too little business context, impose difficult implementations, serve contract-centric rather than broad in-house workflows, and make limited use of stored contract data. Vendors consequently emphasise interoperability, lower implementation burden and AI-driven access to contract intelligence. Material variation concerns architecture and incumbent survival: some forecast AI-first review tools, direct AI over document stores or a distinct legal-department platform category displacing conventional CLM; others propose AI layers integrated with existing repositories; and incumbent vendors argue that CLM can remain foundational through incremental AI embedding, category expansion or ground-up rebuilding. These positions are compatible with the synthesis’s unresolved comparison of replacement, integration and adaptation rather than evidence that one model is superior. Much of the support consists of vendor-reported experiences, product claims and forecasts, with limited independent comparative measurement.

elens.an: The 2023–2024 source supports the proposition’s incumbent-adaptation strand. Jason Boehmig presents Ironclad’s response to generative AI as product-by-product integration into an existing scaled CLM platform, with adoption governed by whether AI creates user value. This is consistent with the synthesis’s view that incumbent products may adapt rather than necessarily be displaced. The source’s material internal distinction is between the interviewer’s framing—competitive pressure, customer trust, incumbent scale and uncertainty about technical readiness—and Boehmig’s own operating principle of selective, value-led embedding. It does not address the cluster’s broader criticisms of siloed, input-heavy CLM systems, nor does it provide comparative evidence showing that incremental integration is superior to replacement or ground-up rebuilding. Its claims are therefore supportive but limited to one route within the unresolved architectural dispute.

The curated 2025 sources collectively accept the proposition that AI is challenging legacy, siloed CLM products without removing businesses’ underlying need for contract infrastructure. Their common reasoning is that incumbent architectures and workflows are difficult to retrofit, legal teams still require contract storage and workflow automation, and rapid technological change is causing buyers to reconsider conventional CLM purchases and long commitments. They materially develop the proposition by identifying concrete adaptation paths—ground-up rebuilding, acquisition of AI-first capability, specialist tools expanding into CLM functions, and conversational systems built on existing CLM foundations—and by extending the adaptation imperative beyond CLM to legal-research vendors and talent-based ALSPs. Material internal variation concerns architecture and continuity: some predict AI-review entrants will absorb CLM functions or displace weak incumbents; Bijapur instead expects current CLM capabilities to remain the foundation; others leave incumbent survival unresolved and favour priorities-led toolkits rather than a single category. The sources also distinguish practical utility from proven market success: funding signals, acquisition anecdotes, reported user enthusiasm and product forecasts do not establish comparative performance, scalable adoption or durable vendor economics. None clearly rejects the proposition, but the evidence is predominantly strategic judgment, implementation experience and prediction rather than independent measurement.

qs.q: You know, look, I helped Screens.AI sell to Agiloft earlier this year on this premise.
qs.a: E27 - Zach and Richard's Legal AI Adventure: Big Deals and AI Revolution · Market & press · 2025

qs.q: I think we are in very much like in the crosshairs and need to adapt not because we're going to be automated out of a job, but just because the standards in general and the expectations of what people want is changing so rapidly.
qs.a: E30 - Is AI Disrupting ALSPs? Axiom CSO Catherine Kemnitz · AI-native providers · 2025

elens.an: The curated 2026 sources support the proposition that AI is challenging siloed, input-heavy CLM products without eliminating the underlying need for contract infrastructure. Common reasons include weak usability, costly or burdensome implementation, failure to retain business context, narrow contract-centric scope, and competition with legal AI for budgets and implementation capacity. Material variation concerns the route forward: Ziniti anticipates both CLM integration and some companies bypassing CLM for AI over document stores; Fleisher combines overlay integration with possible replacement; Jung advocates ground-up rebuilding; Ironclad presents incremental AI embedding within an incumbent CLM; and the Wordsmith discussion proposes a broader, purpose-built legal-department category. Other sources extend the practical analysis to interoperability, new AI change-management demands, and collaborative product stickiness. These accounts do not establish which architecture performs best: much of the evidence consists of practitioner observations, vendor-reported adoption or performance claims, customer anecdotes, and forecasts rather than independent comparative testing. The selection should therefore be read as aligned arguments with meaningful internal variation, not as evidence of how prevalent any view is across the market.
